newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia housing data shows '97 recovery on track.
newsitem.headline: Australia housing data shows '97 recovery on track.

text.p: Australia's housing sector shook off some of the doubts about its 1997 recovery after a strong rise in April housing finance approvals and analysts pointed to a rise in new housing as a sign of better things to come.
Housing finance approvals rose 12.2 percent in April, official data on Wednesday showed. The rise took approvals to 43,595, their highest level since July 1994.
"Today's figures help confirm that the pick up in housing activity over late 1996-early 1997 remains intact," Westpac senior economist John Peters said.
The April rise followed falls of 1.5 percent in March and 6.9 percent in February, and was the largest monthly rise since the 12.4 percent rise in December 1993.
However, there was little market reaction as a strong rise had been widely expected following the release of Australian Bankers Association data last week showing a 12.6 percent rise.
Most pleasing for analysts, and the housing industry, was signs of some strength in the key sectors of construction and the purchase of newly erected dwellings.
Refinancing remains strong, accounting for 24 percent of total loans in April, but excluding refinancing approvals still rose 6.5 percent in the month.
"Today's figures indicate that in a generally sluggish economy there is some confidence in real estate," Real Estate Institute of Australia chief executive Philip Eliason said in a statement.
Within the total rise, approvals for construction rose 12.1 percent, while lending for newly erected dwellings rose 24.3 percent. These sectors make up around 19 percent of approvals.
These two sectors rose a combined 15.3 percent in April to be up 18.4 percent over the last year, and at their highest level since late 1994.

They are seen as important because unlike lending for established housing, or lending to refinance existing loans, lending for construction and newly erected dwellings will flow through to job creation and economic growth.
Purchases of existing dwellings may have some flow through into retail spending, but it is new housing which will be the main driver of the housing industry and add most to growth.
"Anyone with a growth forecast of four-plus percent requires a surge in housing investment, and data like today help considerably," Citibank senior economist Annette Beacher said.
The recovery is expected to be further fuelled by the latest reduction in official rates on May 23, which has flowed through to lower mortgage rates.
However, continued high unemployment is expected to prevent a rapid accleration in the sector, as has been seen in previous upswings.
